\chapter{Evaluation}
\label{ch:results}

Chapter~\ref{ch:setup} fixed what was run --- three models, four
scenarios, three frameworks, one sample per cell. This chapter asks what
it shows. Rather than walking through the 36 cells one at a time, it is
organised around six research questions that each aggregate across every
cell, model, and scenario collected, closing with a synthesis that draws
the six answers together and connects them back to the thesis's central
question (Section~\ref{sec:intro-missing}): \emph{can an LLM agent
iteratively optimise the deployment configuration of a backend application
on a Kubernetes cluster, guided by runtime performance feedback, to
maximise sustainable throughput under fixed infrastructure constraints?}

One methodological finding cuts across several of the research questions
below and is stated once, prominently, here rather than re-derived every
time it is relevant: \textbf{a third of the cells in this dataset were
touched by an LLM-provider billing or quota exhaustion event during
baseline code generation}, and every cell that never reached a working
baseline in this dataset was one of them. Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3}
gives the full accounting; RQ1, RQ4, and RQ6 flag it locally wherever a
number would otherwise be misread as a capability or framework finding.


% ----- §5.1 Overview -----
\section{Overview of the Collected Data}
\label{sec:results-overview}

This chapter reports on \textbf{36 Kubernetes experiments} spanning three
models --- \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}, \texttt{gpt-5.5}, and \texttt{glm-5.2}
--- fully crossed with the four scenarios and three frameworks of
Chapter~\ref{ch:setup} (12 cells per model), one sample per cell, run
under the \texttt{k8s-explore-refine} load profile with a ten-iteration
refinement budget ($N{=}10$).

All figures and summary statistics are produced by a single aggregation
script (\texttt{scripts/analysis/aggregate\_evaluation.py}), which walks
every experiment tree under \texttt{results/} and tabulates per-iteration
goodput, refinement lever, deployment-spec knobs, and recorded failure
records.
%
\textbf{Caveat on sample size.} Every cell in this chapter is a single
sample (one code-generation seed) run once (Section~\ref{sec:setup-procedure}).
The comparisons below are therefore \emph{descriptive}, not statistically
tested; medians and individual scenario-level points are shown side by
side throughout so the reader can judge dispersion directly rather than
trust a single summary statistic. Section~\ref{sec:discussion-limitations}
returns to what this does and does not license us to claim, alongside the
billing-quota confound just introduced above.


% ----- §5.2 RQ1 -----
\section{RQ1: Does Iterative Refinement Improve Sustained Goodput?}
\label{sec:results-rq1}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=1\linewidth]{figures/eval/goodput_trajectories_grid.pdf}
  \caption{Sustained goodput per iteration, one panel per scenario$\times$framework
    cell, coloured by model. A missing line for a model means that model
    never produced a completed baseline bench for that cell --- see
    Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3} before reading a missing line as a
    capability gap.}
  \label{fig:results-trajectories-grid}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{figures/eval/baseline_vs_best_by_model.pdf}
  \caption{Median baseline (iteration \texttt{000}) vs.\ best-refined-iteration
    goodput, per model. Bars show the per-model median across cells; dots show
    every individual scenario$\times$framework cell.}
  \label{fig:results-baseline-vs-best}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evidence.}
Table~\ref{tab:results-rq1-summary} and Figures~\ref{fig:results-trajectories-grid}--\ref{fig:results-baseline-vs-best}
summarise all 36 cells at the model level.

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{Baseline vs.\ best-iteration goodput, by model (median over all
    cells; $n$ = number of scenario$\times$framework cells; ``healthy'' =
    baseline goodput $>0$). Figures are the raw dataset, including cells
    touched by the billing/quota confound of Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3};
    read the healthy-baseline gain column together with the prose below,
    not in isolation.}
  \label{tab:results-rq1-summary}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrrr@{}}
    \toprule
    \textbf{Model} & $n$ cells & Median baseline & Median best & Baseline $>0$ & Median gain (healthy) \\
    \midrule
    \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} & 12 & 2{,}119.0 & 11{,}484.1 & 6 / 12 & $7.2\times$ \\
    \texttt{gpt-5.5}         & 12 & 5{,}224.4 & 32{,}769.8 & 8 / 12 & $2.6\times$ \\
    \texttt{glm-5.2}         & 12 & 0.0       & 13{,}007.9 & 2 / 12 & $8.2\times$ \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

Restricting to cells where the baseline already reached measurable
goodput, the ratio of best-iteration to baseline goodput is positive for
every model. \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s median healthy-baseline gain is $2.6\times$
(mean $15.6\times$, pulled up by a $75.4\times$ outlier on
\textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http}, where the baseline was
severely under-provisioned at 48 replicas and 1 full CPU each, against a
$1.2\times$ floor on \textsc{BranchWeave}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix}, whose
baseline was already close to its achievable ceiling); \texttt{glm-5.2}'s
median is $8.2\times$ over its two healthy cells; \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s
is $7.2\times$ over six healthy cells, ranging from $1.0\times$ to
$16.2\times$. The $1.0\times$ floor (\textsc{Recipes}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask})
is itself a billing-confound artefact, not a genuine refinement-quality
data point: that cell's baseline succeeded but every subsequent iteration
attempt hit the same provider-side quota error before the ten-iteration
budget ran out, so refinement was never actually given a clean attempt.
Excluding it, \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s healthy-cell gain ranges
$1.7$--$16.2\times$ with a median of $11.3\times$. \textbf{TODO: with
two, five (six minus the confounded one), and eight healthy-baseline
cells respectively, none of these medians should be read as more than a
single-digit-sample estimate; re-check once more samples land and the
confounded cells are re-run.}

\paragraph{Refinement also rescues \emph{dead} baselines --- where it gets
the chance to.} In several cells the baseline never reaches a sustained
plateau at all: the adaptive load profile's warm-up step fails its health
check and the explore phase never starts
(Section~\ref{sec:methods-load-profile}), so sustained goodput is recorded
as exactly $0$\,req/s even though some requests were technically served
during the failed warm-up window. Iterative refinement recovers a working,
benchmarkable deployment in \textbf{all 4 of \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s} dead
baselines. \texttt{glm-5.2} has 4 dead baselines, of which 4 recover;
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8} has 2, of which 1 recovers (\textsc{Petstore}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask},
$0\to4{,}053$\,req/s) and 1 does not
(\textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask}, $0\to0$, no refinement
iteration ever produced a passing bench). This is a qualitatively
different contribution than the tuning gains above: it is the loop
converting a \emph{non-functional} deployment into a \emph{functional}
one, not just a faster one --- though, as the one non-recovering case
shows, not a guarantee.

\paragraph{Improvement is not perfectly monotonic.}
Individual iterations regularly regress goodput relative to the previous
successful iteration (visible as sawtooth segments in
Figure~\ref{fig:results-trajectories-grid}). Because the framework only
advances the ``latest good'' lineage on \emph{successful} benches
(Section~\ref{sec:methods-outcome}), a regression is not silently
compounded: the next iteration's decision stage sees it in its feedback,
and in every case observed here the trajectory recovers within one to two
iterations.

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
Iterative refinement improves sustained goodput in essentially every cell
that gets a genuine, uninterrupted opportunity to run --- the exceptions
in this dataset trace to interrupted LLM access, not to the refinement
loop failing on its own terms. The size of the multiplicative gain is
dominated by how badly under-provisioned the baseline happened to be,
which is closer to a property of the baseline LLM call than of the
refinement loop itself.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
\textbf{Yes, with two caveats.} Refinement improves goodput in every
model whenever it gets to run cleanly, and in a majority of cells it is
not a marginal improvement but the difference between a non-functional
and a functional deployment. The size of the multiplicative gain is not a
fixed ``refinement value-add'' comparable across cells; and, separately,
this dataset's completion figures are confounded by provider billing
exhaustion (Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3}), so the ``Baseline $>0$''
column of Table~\ref{tab:results-rq1-summary} should not be read as a
capability ranking.


% ----- §5.3 RQ2 -----
\section{RQ2: Which Refinement Lever Contributes More: Code or Deployment?}
\label{sec:results-rq2}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.75\linewidth]{figures/eval/code_vs_spec_delta.pdf}
  \caption{Per-step goodput change (\%) relative to the previous
    \emph{successful} iteration, split by refinement lever. Steps whose
    predecessor had zero sustained goodput are excluded here (their delta
    is undefined as a percentage) and discussed under RQ1/RQ6.}
  \label{fig:results-code-vs-spec}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evidence.}
Across all three models, 113 completed iterations chose \textbf{code}
refinement and 96 chose \textbf{deployment (spec)} refinement.
Table~\ref{tab:results-rq2-summary} and Figure~\ref{fig:results-code-vs-spec}
break the resulting per-step goodput change down by model and lever.

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{Per-step goodput change (\%) by refinement lever and model
    (excludes steps whose predecessor had zero goodput).}
  \label{tab:results-rq2-summary}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrrrr@{}}
    \toprule
    & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{Code}} & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{Spec}} \\
    \textbf{Model} & $n$ & median & mean & $n$ & median & mean \\
    \midrule
    \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} & 23 & $+4.9\%$ & $+12.4\%$ & 24 & $+2.6\%$ & $-2.0\%$ \\
    \texttt{gpt-5.5}         & 35 & $+6.7\%$ & $+36.2\%$ & 43 & $+1.2\%$ & $-1.2\%$ \\
    \texttt{glm-5.2}         & 14 & $+0.3\%$ & $+1.8\%$  & 17 & $+1.4\%$ & $+2.9\%$ \\
    \midrule
    \textbf{All}             & 72 & $+4.3\%$ & $+21.9\%$ & 84 & $+1.5\%$ & $-0.6\%$ \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Code refinement has a heavier tail; spec refinement is a
smaller, noisier knob --- for two of the three models.} Pooled across all
models, median per-step change is similar and modest for both levers
(code $+4.3\%$, spec $+1.5\%$), but the \emph{mean} diverges sharply
(code $+21.9\%$, spec $-0.6\%$). The gap is driven by a handful of large
code-side recoveries --- single-step jumps of up to $+334.9\%$
(\texttt{gpt-5.5}) and $+194.9\%$ (\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}) --- where a
code change fixed a latent correctness or connection-handling bug that no
amount of replica or resource tuning could have addressed. Deployment
refinement, once the application is already healthy, behaves like what it
is designed to be: a marginal capacity/placement adjustment, occasionally
negative, for example an overly aggressive resource cut or a
connection-pool change that backfires (Section~\ref{sec:results-rq6}).
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s mean code effect ($+12.4\%$) is noticeably
lower than \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s ($+36.2\%$) despite a comparable median;
part of this gap is the billing-affected cells, whose few surviving
iterations are noisier than a clean trajectory's would be
(Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3}), so this specific comparison should be
treated as provisional pending a re-run.

\texttt{glm-5.2} is the clearest exception to the ``code has the heavier
tail'' reading: its code-refinement median ($+0.3\%$) is barely
distinguishable from its spec-refinement median ($+1.4\%$), and its spec
mean is positive where the other two models' is negative. With only 14
code and 17 spec steps recorded for this model, the more defensible
reading is that \texttt{glm-5.2} simply produces smaller code edits per
step, not that the lever asymmetry seen in the other two models is
absent in general.

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
This supports the framework's decision to keep code and deployment
refinement mutually exclusive per iteration
(Section~\ref{sec:methods-workflow}): the two levers act on genuinely
different failure classes across the two higher-cost models. Code
refinement does more of the heavy lifting for correctness-adjacent
bottlenecks --- the same class of bug BaxBench's original single-container
evaluation cannot even observe, since it never applies load
(Section~\ref{sec:rw-benchmarks}); deployment refinement does
comparatively fine-grained capacity tuning once the application is
already sound. \texttt{glm-5.2}'s flatter profile is consistent with a
weaker model making smaller, more conservative edits on both levers
rather than with the two-levers-different-jobs story breaking down.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
\textbf{Code refinement contributes the largest single-step gains and
carries most of the ``fix a broken deployment'' work; deployment
refinement is a smaller, more consistent, occasionally negative capacity
knob.} This division of labour holds clearly for \texttt{gpt-5.5} and,
more provisionally, for \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}; \texttt{glm-5.2}'s
smaller, flatter steps on both levers suggest the asymmetry itself may be
a function of model capability rather than a property of the two levers
in general.


% ----- §5.4 RQ3 -----
\section{RQ3: How Do the Models Compare?}
\label{sec:results-rq3}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.75\linewidth]{figures/eval/completion_funnel.pdf}
  \caption{Run completion status per model, counted over scenario$\times$framework
    cells. ``Aborted at baseline'' = baseline code or spec generation never
    produced a completed bench. \textbf{Most of this category in this
    dataset is a billing/quota artefact, not a model failure} --- see text.
    ``Completed full trajectory'' = reached iteration 010.}
  \label{fig:results-completion-funnel}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evidence: the raw completion numbers.}
\texttt{gpt-5.5} reaches a completed baseline bench in \textbf{12/12}
cells and completes the full ten-iteration trajectory in \textbf{12/12}.
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8} reaches a completed baseline in \textbf{8/12}
cells, completing the full trajectory in all 8. \texttt{glm-5.2} reaches
a completed baseline in \textbf{6/12} cells, completing the full
trajectory in all 6.

\paragraph{Evidence: what actually explains the gap.}
Reading those numbers as a capability ranking would be a mistake. Every
one of the ten cells that never reached baseline in this dataset ---
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s 4 and \texttt{glm-5.2}'s 6, all of it --- shows
a provider-side billing or quota exhaustion error
(\texttt{llm\_call}-kind failures whose recorded error text is, verbatim,
Anthropic's ``credit balance is too low to access the Anthropic API'',
Z.ai's ``This request requires more credits, or fewer max\_tokens'', or
comparable) recorded against every single generation attempt for that
cell, up to the baseline retry limit. None of these ten cells shows a
single \texttt{functional\_test} failure or any other correctness-related
signal --- the model was never actually given a working LLM connection
long enough to generate code that could be judged. A further three cells
(\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s \textsc{Recipes}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask},
\texttt{gpt-5.5}'s \textsc{Recipes}$\times$\textsc{Rust-Actix}, and
\texttt{glm-5.2}'s \textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask}) hit
the same class of error partway through but eventually recovered --- their
completed-iteration counts are 3, 3, and 5 out of a possible 11, well
below the 10--11 every unaffected cell reaches, so their per-cell cost
and iteration-count figures elsewhere in this chapter are inflated by
wasted retries, even though their final goodput numbers are real
measurements. \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s 0/12 non-completion rate is therefore
best read as ``this account's credits happened not to run out during
this model's runs,'' not as evidence \texttt{gpt-5.5} is more reliable at
generating working code.

\paragraph{Cost.} Measured LLM spend (Table~\ref{tab:setup-model-cost})
still shows \texttt{glm-5.2} roughly an order of magnitude cheaper per
cell than \texttt{gpt-5.5} or \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}, but this figure is
now visibly contaminated by the same confound: a cell that fails ten
consecutive baseline attempts on a billing error accrues little or no
LLM spend (failed calls are rejected before generating billable output),
so \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s and \texttt{glm-5.2}'s per-cell averages
are pulled down by cells that were never really attempted, not by cells
that were attempted cheaply. \textbf{TODO: recompute cost per
\emph{completed} cell only once the confounded cells are re-run, and
separately report cost-per-wasted-attempt as its own number --- the
current \$/cell figures conflate ``efficient'' with ``never got to
spend.''}

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
With the confound identified, this dataset provides \emph{much weaker}
evidence about relative model capability than a first read of the
completion funnel suggests. What can still be said with reasonable
confidence: among cells that were genuinely attempted (excluding the ten
fully-lost ones), every model reaches a working baseline on effectively
all of them --- \texttt{gpt-5.5} 12/12, \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} 8/8,
\texttt{glm-5.2} 6/6 --- and all three go on to refine substantially once
alive (Section~\ref{sec:results-rq1}). The honest reading of RQ3 in this
dataset is therefore closer to ``we cannot yet distinguish these three
models' baseline-generation reliability'' than to any ranking.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
\textbf{This dataset does not support a capability ranking between the
three models on completion rate}, because the observed differences trace
entirely to when each model's provider account ran low on funds during
data collection, not to generation quality. What it does support: once a
cell is genuinely attempted, all three models reach a working baseline
and go on to refine it substantially, which is itself a more useful
finding than a spurious ranking would have been. Closing this gap
properly requires re-running the thirteen affected cells with a funded
account and is the single most important item in
Section~\ref{sec:conclusion-future-work}.


% ----- §5.5 RQ4 -----
\section{RQ4: Does Framework/Language Choice Affect Achievable Goodput?}
\label{sec:results-rq4}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{figures/eval/framework_comparison.pdf}
  \caption{Best goodput reached per framework (symlog $y$-axis), split by
    model. Each dot is one scenario cell; the horizontal bar is the
    per-model median for that framework. Zero-dot bars
    (\texttt{claude-opus-4-8} and \texttt{glm-5.2} on
    \textsc{Rust-Actix}) are the billing/quota confound of
    Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3}, not a framework-difficulty finding.}
  \label{fig:results-framework-comparison}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evidence.}
\textsc{Go-net-http} reaches the highest goodput for all three models
(medians $56{,}048$\,req/s for \texttt{gpt-5.5}, $36{,}844$\,req/s for
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}, $17{,}845$\,req/s for \texttt{glm-5.2}),
consistent with a compiled, natively-concurrent runtime under CPU-bound
load. \textsc{Python-Flask} trails on all three models (medians
$20{,}260$, $2{,}961$, and $7{,}210$\,req/s respectively --- the
\texttt{claude-opus-4-8} figure is pulled down by its
\textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask} dead cell,
Section~\ref{sec:results-rq1}), in line with the expected throughput
ceiling of a single-process WSGI stack under \texttt{gunicorn}, even
after the agent tunes replica count and worker/pool sizing.
\textsc{Rust-Actix} cannot be compared at all for two of the three
models: \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} and \texttt{glm-5.2} show zero
benchmarkable \textsc{Rust-Actix} cells out of four each, and --- unlike
what an earlier reading of this same gap concluded --- \textbf{this is
not a framework-correctness finding.} Every one of those eight cells'
recorded failures is the billing/quota confound of
Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3}, not a \texttt{functional\_test} failure;
the models were never given a completed LLM call to generate
\textsc{Rust-Actix} code from. \texttt{gpt-5.5} is the only model with
usable \textsc{Rust-Actix} data (median $33{,}147$\,req/s, competitive
with its own \textsc{Go-net-http} figure), and even one of its four
\textsc{Rust-Actix} cells (\textsc{Recipes}) hit the same billing error
repeatedly before eventually recovering.

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
The \textsc{Go-net-http} $>$ \textsc{Python-Flask} ceiling ordering is
genuine and consistent across all three models, and is readable as a
runtime-throughput effect independent of refinement. The apparent
\textsc{Rust-Actix} gap is not: this chapter cannot currently say whether
\textsc{Rust-Actix} is harder, easier, or no different from the other two
frameworks for \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} or \texttt{glm-5.2}, because
neither model was ever given a fair, uninterrupted attempt at it.
\textbf{TODO: this is the framework-level analogue of RQ3's finding, and
is resolved by the same re-run.}

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
\textbf{Framework sets an achievable-goodput ceiling}
(\textsc{Go-net-http} $>$ \textsc{Python-Flask} in every model with
usable data) \textbf{that refinement operates within, not around.} The
three-way \textsc{Rust-Actix} comparison this chapter originally set out
to make is not currently answerable from this dataset; it requires
re-running the eight billing-affected \textsc{Rust-Actix} cells, not
further analysis of the existing ones.


% ----- §5.6 RQ5 -----
\section{RQ5: What Deployment Parameters Does the Agent Converge To?}
\label{sec:results-rq5}

\paragraph{Evidence.}
Spec prompts intentionally omit recommended numeric ranges
(Section~\ref{sec:methods-spec}), so any sensible-looking convergence in
\texttt{backend.replicas}, per-pod resource requests, or database
topology is evidence the agent is reading load-test and utilisation
feedback rather than falling back on defaults. The clearest example is
\texttt{gpt-5.5} on \textsc{ClickCount}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http} (the
$75\times$ case from RQ1):

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{Spec-knob trajectory for \texttt{gpt-5.5}, \textsc{ClickCount},
    \textsc{Go-net-http} (selected iterations).}
  \label{tab:results-rq5-clickcount}
  \footnotesize
  \begin{tabular}{@{}rrrrrrr@{}}
    \toprule
    Iter.\ & Lever & Goodput (req/s) & Replicas & CPU req.\ & DB repl.\ & DB max\_conn \\
    \midrule
    000 & baseline & 1{,}285.1  & 48  & 1000m & 3 & 500 \\
    006 & code     & 23{,}670.6 & 48  & 1000m & 3 & 500 \\
    007 & spec     & 23{,}640.9 & 192 & 350m  & 1 & 300 \\
    008 & code     & 90{,}653.8 & 192 & 350m  & 1 & 300 \\
    009 & spec     & 91{,}392.6 & 320 & 250m  & 1 & 500 \\
    010 & code     & 96{,}924.9 & 320 & 250m  & 1 & 500 \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

Between iterations 006 and 010, the agent roughly \emph{sextuples}
replica count (48 $\to$ 320) while \emph{quartering} per-pod CPU request
(1000m $\to$ 250m), trading a few large pods for many small ones, and
drops database replicas from 3 to 1. For a scenario whose endpoints are a
near-stateless counter increment (Section~\ref{sec:setup-scenarios}),
this is the correct qualitative direction: per-request CPU cost is
negligible, so raw horizontal fan-out beats per-pod headroom, and the
extra Postgres read replicas the baseline provisioned were never
load-bearing. \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} shows qualitatively similar
single-step spec jumps (up to $+167.5\%$; Table~\ref{tab:results-rq2-summary})
on its own cells, though a full knob-by-knob trajectory is not reproduced
here. \textbf{TODO: instrument \texttt{kubectl top} utilisation alongside
this table (available in \texttt{05-bench/diagnostics/}) to show the
CPU-utilisation signal that presumably drove this, rather than just
asserting it post hoc.}

Not every spec-refinement decision pays off, however:
Section~\ref{sec:results-rq6} gives a case where the stated rationale is
reasonable but the resulting deployment regresses to zero goodput.

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
Where the agent has enough successful iterations to work with, its
\texttt{spec.yaml} trajectory tracks the workload's actual scaling
characteristics rather than converging on generic defaults, which is the
behaviour the constrained-schema design of Section~\ref{sec:methods-design}
was intended to elicit.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
\textbf{The agent converges on workload-appropriate deployment parameters
when given the room to iterate}, but this chapter has one detailed
example, not a systematic audit; RQ6's counter-example shows this is a
tendency, not a guarantee.


% ----- §5.7 RQ6 -----
\section{RQ6: Failure Modes and Case Studies}
\label{sec:results-rq6}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.75\linewidth]{figures/eval/failure_taxonomy.pdf}
  \caption{Recorded \texttt{failure.json} occurrences by phase and kind,
    summed across all three models and all cells. \texttt{llm\_call}
    entries are dominated by the billing/quota confound of
    Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3}; see text for the split.}
  \label{fig:results-failure-taxonomy}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evidence.}
Of \textbf{61} recorded failures, 24 are \texttt{02-code: functional\_test}
failures --- baseline or refined code that fails \textsc{BaxBench}'s own
functional test suite before an image is ever built --- and these are
the dataset's genuine code-correctness signal. A further \textbf{33} are
\texttt{llm\_call} failures (22 at the decision phase, 10 at the code
phase, 1 at the spec phase); tracing every one of them to its underlying
\texttt{llm\_error} text shows \textbf{32 of the 33} are the provider
billing/quota exhaustion confound of Section~\ref{sec:results-rq3},
concentrated in the thirteen cells identified there
(\texttt{claude-opus-4-8}: 12/12 of its \texttt{llm\_call} failures;
\texttt{glm-5.2}: 12/12; \texttt{gpt-5.5}: 8/9). This is worth stating
plainly: over half of the raw failure count in this dataset is one
operational artefact, not thirty-three independent reliability events.
The 33rd \texttt{llm\_call} failure is a different, genuine stop
condition: \texttt{gpt-5.5}'s \textsc{Petstore}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask}
cell hit its own configured \texttt{--llm-max-cost} ceiling
(\$20.22 spent against a \$20.00 cap) at iteration 010's spec-refinement
attempt --- the framework's cost-tracking safeguard
(Section~\ref{sec:methods-workflow}) doing exactly what it is designed to
do, not a reliability failure. Excluding all of the above, the remaining
signal is: 24 \texttt{functional\_test}, 1 \texttt{docker\_build}, 1
decision-phase \texttt{llm\_parse}, and \textbf{2 new \texttt{04-deploy:
unschedulable}} failures, both on \texttt{claude-opus-4-8}'s
\textsc{Petstore}$\times$\textsc{Python-Flask} cell, both on consecutive
spec-refinement iterations. This is the first deploy-phase failure
recorded anywhere in this evaluation: a proposed spec's resource requests
passed static validation (Section~\ref{sec:methods-spec}) but could not
actually be scheduled onto any node at apply time, which points at a real
gap between the static ``does this fit on \emph{a} worker in isolation''
check and the cluster's actual bin-packing state once other pods are
already running on it --- a genuine, if narrow, framework-level finding
rather than a confound. \texttt{claude-opus-4-8} contributes 16 of the 61
raw failures (12 of them the billing artefact); \texttt{gpt-5.5} and
\texttt{glm-5.2} contribute 22 and 23 (8 and 12 of them billing/cost-cap
artefacts, respectively).

\paragraph{Case study: a connection-pooling bug invisible to
single-container evaluation.} \texttt{glm-5.2}'s
\textsc{Recipes}$\times$\textsc{Go-net-http} baseline reaches a completed
bench but records \textbf{0} sustained goodput: the adaptive profile's
warm-up step fails health checks and explore never starts. Postgres logs
from that run show the deployment producing roughly 937 errors during the
load window, dominated by two error classes:
\texttt{\small unnamed prepared statement does not exist} and
\texttt{\small bind message supplies N parameters, but prepared statement
requires M}. This is the classic symptom of a Go SQL driver using
server-side prepared statements against PgBouncer in \texttt{transaction}
pooling mode, where a prepared statement created on one physical
connection is invisible on the next pooled connection a later query lands
on. This bug is invisible to \textsc{BaxBench}'s original single-container
functional tests (which use a direct, unpooled connection) and only
manifests once the generated code is deployed behind the pooler this
framework introduces. Iteration~001 (code refinement) does not fix it
(goodput remains 0); iteration~002 (code refinement again, chosen freely
by the decision stage given the iteration~001 failure feedback) does,
jumping to $19{,}026.7$\,req/s. This is direct evidence that iterative
\emph{code} refinement, not deployment tuning, is the correct lever for
an infra-interaction bug the model could not have anticipated at
generation time, and that it can take more than one attempt. Unlike the
billing failures above, this one is a genuine, reproducible application
bug --- it has nothing to do with LLM transport.

\paragraph{Case study: a plausible deployment decision that backfires.}
On the same cell, iteration~003's decision stage reasons as follows
(quoted verbatim from its \texttt{decision.json}):
\begin{quote}
\small
``The code is now well-optimized (0\% failures, 19K/s goodput) and the
bottleneck is purely infrastructure: Postgres hits 200/200 connections
with PgBouncer \texttt{cl\_waiting} reaching 311, and db-primary CPU
saturates at 16.7 cores. [...] We should add database replicas, enable a
read pooler, increase Postgres \texttt{max\_connections} and PgBouncer
\texttt{default\_pool\_size}, and potentially reduce over-provisioned
backend CPU to free cluster budget for more DB resources.''
\end{quote}
The reasoning is a coherent read of the previous iteration's diagnostics
(Section~\ref{sec:methods-bench}), and the resulting spec does exactly
what it describes: database replicas 1 $\to$ 3, \texttt{max\_connections}
200 $\to$ 300, backend CPU request 2000m $\to$ 500m. The resulting
deployment, however, regresses to \textbf{0} sustained goodput. The next
iteration (004, code) recovers to $20{,}494$\,req/s \emph{without}
reverting the topology change, so the regression is not explained by the
added replicas alone; most plausibly the simultaneous $4\times$ backend
CPU cut left the application under-provisioned for its own request
handling while the new DB topology was still stabilising.
\textbf{Lesson for the framework, not just the model}: this iteration
changed four spec fields at once, which is consistent with the
single-lever-per-iteration design (Section~\ref{sec:methods-workflow})
but does not prevent \emph{multiple fields within one lever} from
changing simultaneously, which limits attribution within a spec-refinement
step the same way mixing code and spec changes would across steps.

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
Once the billing confound is separated out, the remaining evidence
continues to support the reading from the earlier draft of this chapter:
essentially all \emph{genuine} attrition happens at the code-correctness
gate the agent is directly responsible for, and the cluster-execution
path is close to, but not quite, failure-free --- the two
\texttt{unschedulable} cases are a real, if narrow, gap between static
validation and actual scheduling feasibility. The two case studies
together show the same lesson from opposite directions: code refinement
can fix bugs the model could not have anticipated (the pooling case), and
a single deployment decision can undo a healthy deployment even when its
diagnosis is correct, because the framework does not constrain how many
fields one spec-refinement step may touch (the backfire case).

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
\textbf{The dominant \emph{genuine} failure mode is upstream of
deployment}, in code correctness, exactly as the earlier reading of this
chapter concluded --- but that reading also mis-stated its own evidence
base by treating 32 billing-artefact failures as if they were signal.
With those excluded, the cluster-execution path is nearly, not entirely,
failure-free: two \texttt{unschedulable} deploys point at a real,
fixable gap in static spec validation.


% ----- §5.8 Cross-Cutting Synthesis -----
\section{Cross-Cutting Synthesis}
\label{sec:results-synthesis}

Read together across all 36 cells, three models, and four scenarios,
four patterns recur consistently enough to generalise beyond any single
cell:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Correctness gates deployment, consistently.} Among
        genuine (non-billing) failures, the largest single source of
        attrition (RQ6) and the largest single-step goodput gains (RQ2)
        both trace back to code correctness, not deployment tuning. This
        holds across every model with usable data and is exactly the
        class of bug BaxBench's original single-container evaluation
        cannot observe (Section~\ref{sec:rw-benchmarks}).
  \item \textbf{Deployment refinement is real but bounded.} Across every
        model, spec refinement's median per-step effect is small
        (RQ2: $+1.5\%$ pooled) and occasionally negative, never
        approaching code refinement's heavy tail. Deployment tuning is a
        genuine, but fundamentally marginal-capacity, lever once an
        application is already correct --- not a second path to the
        same order-of-magnitude gains code refinement can produce.
  \item \textbf{This dataset cannot currently distinguish the three
        models' baseline-generation reliability, and the earlier version
        of this chapter overstated that it could.} The completion-rate
        and framework-coverage gaps that looked like capability findings
        (RQ3, RQ4) trace, cell for cell, to provider billing exhaustion
        during data collection. What survives that correction is
        narrower but more solid: all three models refine substantially
        once genuinely alive (RQ1), and \textsc{Go-net-http} $>$
        \textsc{Python-Flask} in achievable ceiling for every model with
        usable data (RQ4).
  \item \textbf{The cluster-execution path is close to, but not quite,
        the one component that never appears as a bottleneck.} Two
        \texttt{unschedulable} deploy failures out of 61 recorded (and
        \emph{zero} bench-phase harness failures) is still strong
        evidence for the framework-owns-infrastructure design principle
        (Section~\ref{sec:methods-design}), with one concrete, narrow
        exception: static spec validation does not currently catch every
        case where a proposed deployment cannot actually be scheduled.
\end{itemize}

The clearest lesson this pass adds to the previous one is methodological
rather than empirical: a coarse failure-kind label
(\texttt{llm\_call}) silently conflated a genuine transport reliability
signal with an entirely separate operational artefact (running out of
provider credits mid-experiment), and the two look identical until the
underlying error text is actually read. Every model-comparison claim in
this thesis that touches completion rate has been checked against that
distinction; Section~\ref{sec:discussion-limitations} generalises the
caution.


% ----- §5.9 Summary -----
\section{Summary}
\label{sec:results-summary}

Across all three models and all 36 scenario/framework cells collected:
%
\begin{itemize}
  \item iterative refinement improves sustained goodput in essentially
        every cell that gets a genuine, uninterrupted attempt, and
        separately rescues most \emph{dead} baselines observed into a
        working deployment (RQ1);
  \item code refinement contributes the largest single-step gains for two
        of three models, dominated by fixes to bugs that only manifest
        under load and cluster topology; deployment refinement is a
        smaller, more consistent, occasionally negative marginal capacity
        knob for all three (RQ2);
  \item \textbf{this dataset does not support a completion-rate capability
        ranking between the three models}: every cell that never reached
        baseline is explained by provider billing/quota exhaustion during
        data collection, not by generation quality (RQ3);
  \item \textsc{Go-net-http} sets the highest achievable-goodput ceiling
        among all three models; the apparent \textsc{Rust-Actix} gap for
        two of three models is the same billing confound, not a
        framework-difficulty finding (RQ4);
  \item where it converges, the agent's deployment-spec trajectory tracks
        workload characteristics sensibly (RQ5), though not every
        individual spec-refinement decision improves the outcome, even
        when its stated rationale is sound (RQ6);
  \item nearly all \emph{genuine} attrition happens at the
        code-correctness gate the agent is responsible for; the
        cluster-execution path is nearly, not entirely, failure-free,
        with one narrow gap between static spec validation and actual
        scheduling feasibility (RQ6).
\end{itemize}

These findings are discussed further, including limitations and threats
to validity, in Chapter~\ref{ch:discussion}, and answered directly against
the thesis's research question in Chapter~\ref{ch:conclusion}.
